topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: A Topological Journey
target_audience: University undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry

outline.topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: A Topological Journey
outline.target_audience: University undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry

sections.title: Introduction: The Table on the Uneven Floor
sections.content: Introduce the core concept using a relatable analogy. Imagine an explorer, 'Leo the Lion', trying to place a four-legged square table on a wobbly, uneven looping path. Can Leo always find a spot where all four legs touch the path simultaneously?
sections.example: Visualizing a flexible rubber band (the curve) and a rigid square frame (the table). No matter how you warp the rubber band, can the square's corners always stay on the line?

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Jordan Curves
sections.content: Define a 'Jordan Curve'—a simple closed loop that doesn't intersect itself. Explain that we are looking for four points on this curve that form the vertices of a square or rectangle.
sections.example: Animation showing a circle being deformed into a 'blob' shape. As long as it doesn't snap or cross itself, it remains a Jordan curve.

sections.title: The Geometry of Pairs: Mapping to 3D Space
sections.content: Introduce the 'Configuration Space' method. Instead of looking at the curve, we look at every possible pair of points (A, B) on the curve. We map these pairs to a 3D coordinate (x, y, z) where (x,y) is the midpoint of the chord AB, and z is the distance between them.
sections.example: A point 'P' moving along a 3D surface as two dots crawl along the perimeter of a 2D shape. The height of 'P' represents how far apart the two dots are.

sections.title: The Topological Twist: Creating the Möbius Strip
sections.content: Explain that the space of all unordered pairs of points on a circle forms a Möbius Strip. This is the 'Aha!' moment of the proof for the inscribed rectangle. If we plot the midpoints and distances of all pairs, they form a surface bounded by the original curve.
sections.example: An animation showing a flat sheet of paper being twisted and glued into a Möbius Strip to represent the mathematical 'state space' of the pairs of points.

sections.title: The Intersection: Proving the Rectangle exists
sections.content: Show that the surface generated by the curve must intersect itself or a specific plane if the curve is 'projected' correctly. Using the property of the Möbius Strip's boundary, we prove that there must be two different pairs of points with the same midpoint and same distance—forming a rectangle.
sections.example: Two different chords (AB and CD) sharing the same center point and having equal length, forming the diagonals of a rectangle.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Unsolved Square Peg Problem
sections.content: Summarize that while we've proven a rectangle always exists for any smooth loop (The Rectangle Peg Problem), the 'Square Peg Problem' (Toeplitz's Conjecture) remains one of the most famous partially solved mysteries for certain types of curves.
sections.example: A gallery of diverse shapes (stars, blobs, heart shapes) each showing a successfully inscribed square, ending with a question mark over a 'fractal' curve.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Table on the Uneven Floor
lecture_lines: Imagine a square table on an uneven loop.
Can all four legs touch the path simultaneously?
This is the famous Inscribed Square Problem.
The loop is a flexible Jordan curve.
We seek four points forming square vertices.
animations: Create a white (#FFFFFF) Jordan curve as an irregular loop in the center.
Create a square with red (#FF0000) vertices and place it near the loop.
Animate the square moving and rotating, with vertices occasionally missing the curve.
Transform the loop into a different irregular closed shape.
Highlight the square with a pulse effect when all four red vertices lie on the curve.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Jordan Curves
lecture_lines: A Jordan curve is a simple closed loop.
It never crosses itself and has no gaps.
Any shape can be deformed into this loop.
animations: Draw a cyan (#00FFFF) circle in the center of the frame.
Animate the transformation of the circle into a non-self-intersecting irregular blob.
Display the text 'Jordan Curve' in yellow (#FFFF00) and the text 'Simple & Closed' below it.

storyboard.title: The Geometry of Pairs: Mapping to 3D Space
lecture_lines: Map every pair of points to 3D space.
The xy-coordinate is the pair's midpoint.
The height represents the distance between points.
These points form a continuous surface in space.
Each surface point represents a unique chord.
animations: Draw a white (#FFFFFF) Jordan curve with two points A and B labeled in green (#00FF00).
Draw a line segment between A and B and its midpoint M labeled in orange (#FFA500).
Draw a vertical line from M with height proportional to the length of segment AB.
Animate the tip of the vertical line tracing a continuous path as A and B move along the curve.
Fade in a translucent purple (#800080) surface representing all possible point pairs.

storyboard.title: The Topological Twist: Creating the Möbius Strip
lecture_lines: Unordered pairs create a mathematical twist.
This configuration space forms a Möbius strip.
The curve forms the strip's single boundary.
This topological property is key to our proof.
We seek intersections within this twisted space.
animations: Show a flat rectangular strip in lavender (#E6E6FA) in a 3D-like perspective.
Mark the left and right edges with red (#FF0000) arrows pointing in opposite directions.
Animate the strip twisting 180 degrees in the center.
Merge the edges to form a 3D Möbius strip.
Highlight the single continuous boundary of the Möbius strip in yellow (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: The Intersection: Proving the Rectangle exists
lecture_lines: A rectangle's diagonals have equal length and midpoint.
The surface's topology forces a self-intersection point.
This intersection guarantees an inscribed rectangle exists.
animations: Show the Möbius strip surface from the previous section in a 3D coordinate space.
Highlight a self-intersection point where two different chords share the same midpoint and length.
Transition back to the 2D loop and draw the two equal chords forming a rectangle in gold (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Conclusion: The Unsolved Square Peg Problem
lecture_lines: Every smooth loop contains an inscribed rectangle.
Finding a square remains a famous mystery.
Topology reveals hidden structures within simple shapes.
animations: Display a grid of shapes (star, heart, ellipse) each containing an inscribed gold (#FFD700) square.
Morph the grid into a single complex fractal curve with a large red (#FF0000) question mark.
Fade out everything and display the text 'Toeplitz\'s Conjecture' in white (#FFFFFF).
